notes.meaning: God commands His people never to spread false rumors or tell lies about other people. An honest person must not team up with an evil person by giving dishonest testimony in a legal case. The person who listens to and repeats a slanderous story causes just as much harm as the one who made it up.

God warns against going along with the majority when they are doing something wrong. When testifying in court, a person must never twist the truth just to please the crowd or agree with powerful leaders. Standing alone for what is right is always better than following a crowd into sin.

Courts must be guided by truth and fairness rather than pity. A judge or witness must not favor a poor man in his lawsuit if he is actually in the wrong. Justice must be based on facts and God's law, not on a person's social standing.

If an Israelite finds an enemy's lost ox or donkey wandering away, he is required to take it back safely. If he sees an enemy's donkey collapsed under a heavy load, he must stop and help get the animal on its feet. God commands His people to show practical mercy and kindness even to people who hate them.

While judges must not favor the poor wrongly, they must never deny them fair treatment either. A person's poverty should never be an excuse to cheat them out of an honest decision. God protects the vulnerable by demanding equal justice for all.

God commands His people to stay far away from dishonest schemes and untrue charges. Courts must never put an innocent or upright person to death through false testimony. God reminds human judges that He sees everything and will never clear the guilty.

Judges and leaders must never accept a bribe. Secret gifts corrupt the mind, blinding people who would otherwise see clearly and twisting the words of honest men. Refusing bribes protects the fairness of the legal system and honors God.

The Israelites are forbidden to mistreat or take advantage of foreigners living among them. They knew firsthand the pain, fear, and loneliness of being treated badly in Egypt. That experience was meant to give them tender hearts and fair practices toward outsiders.

The people were to plant and harvest their fields, vineyards, and olive groves for six years, but let the land rest during the seventh year. Whatever grew on its own in that year was left for the poor to eat, and wild animals could eat what remained. This law taught the people to depend on God's provision and reminded them that He owned the land.

God repeats the rule that work must stop on the seventh day of each week. This regular day of rest gave physical relief and renewed strength to working animals, family members, and servants. God cares about the bodily well-being of all living creatures under our care.

The Lord tells His people to pay careful attention to every instruction He has given. They were not even to speak the names of pagan gods or use them in oaths. Complete devotion to the true God leaves no room for honoring idols in speech or thought.

God set apart three annual religious festivals for the nation to celebrate before Him. These national gatherings gave the people regular seasons to stop work and rejoice together in God's goodness. They strengthened the unity of the twelve tribes and kept true worship alive.

The first festival was the Feast of Unleavened Bread, held in the spring month of Abib to recall the escape from Egyptian slavery. For seven days the people ate bread made without yeast, just as their ancestors did on the night of the exodus. Every worshiper was expected to bring an offering rather than appear before the Lord empty-handed.

The second festival was the Feast of Harvest, celebrating the first crops gathered from the spring planting. The third was the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the agricultural year, when all the grain, fruit, and olives had been stored. These gatherings were joyous times to thank God for the food He faithfully provided.

Three times every year, all the men of Israel were to gather at the Lord's chosen place of worship. This regular pilgrimage renewed their covenant loyalty to God as their King and heavenly Protector. Even while the men were away, God watched over their homes and defended their borders.

God commands that the blood of His festival sacrifices must never be offered alongside bread containing yeast. In addition, the choice fat of the festival sacrifice could not be left out overnight until the morning. The best parts of the offering belonged solely to God and had to be treated with great respect.

Worshipers were to bring the very first and best produce of their soil to the house of the Lord as a gift of thanksgiving. God also told them never to boil a young goat in its mother's milk. Giving the first portion to God showed that the people trusted Him to provide for the rest of their needs.

differ.view: This rule forbids killing or cooking a young goat before it has been weaned from its mother's milk.
This rule forbids cooking an animal in its own mother's milk because doing so is an unnatural cruelty that defiles sacred sacrifices and common meals.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars view this rule as a ban on a specific pagan fertility ritual in which a kid was boiled in milk and sprinkled on crops to make the land productive.

notes.meaning: God promises to send an angel ahead of Israel to protect them on their travels through the wilderness. This divine guide would lead the people safely into the land that God had already prepared for them. Christian teachers have long understood this angel to be Christ Himself watching over His people before His birth on earth.

The people were told to listen carefully to this angel and never rebel against him. Because God's own Name and nature resided in him, he held full divine authority to judge their deeds. Disobeying this messenger was the same as defying God Himself.

God promised that if the people obeyed the angel's voice and kept His commandments, He would stand with them completely. He would treat Israel's enemies as His own personal foes. Their safety and victory depended on their willingness to trust and follow God.

God's angel would lead the Israelites straight into the land held by the pagan nations of Canaan. Because of those nations' persistent evil, God promised to wipe them out before Israel. The Israelites were to know that their coming victory was God's doing, not their own.

Israel was forbidden to bow to Canaanite idols, serve them, or copy the wicked religious practices of the land. Instead, they had to tear down the pagan shrines and smash their sacred stone pillars to bits. God's people were to make a clean break from every form of false worship.

If Israel served the Lord faithfully, He promised to bless their daily food and water so that simple provisions would sustain them. He also promised to remove severe illnesses from their midst. God pledged to provide for both their physical needs and their bodily health.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critical scholars suggest that verses 23 through the middle of verse 25 were added by later editors rather than being part of the original passage.

notes.meaning: God promised that no woman or farm animal in the land would miscarry or be unable to bear young. He also assured His people that they would live out the full number of their years without their lives being cut short. Obedience to God would result in flourishing life across the entire community.

The Lord promised to send a deep dread ahead of Israel that would throw enemy armies into wild panic. When opposing forces tried to stand against Israel, that fear would cause them to turn around and flee. God won the battles by taking away the courage of the enemy.

God promised to send the hornet ahead of His people to drive the Canaanite nations out of their path. Some readers see this as literal swarms of stinging insects, while others see it as a picture of sharp, stinging terror that drove the enemies away. God can use even the smallest means to defeat powerful armies.

God explained that He would not drive out all the inhabitants in a single year. If the land emptied out too quickly, fields would turn wild and dangerous beasts would multiply against the small population of Israelites. Therefore, God drove out the nations step by step as Israel grew large enough to occupy the territory.

God laid out the full boundaries of the promised land, reaching from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean and from the southern desert to the Euphrates River. He promised to hand the native inhabitants over so that Israel could drive them out. This expansive promise reached its fullest earthly realization during the reigns of King David and King Solomon.

The Israelites were strictly forbidden from making treaties or peace pacts with the pagan peoples or their gods. Forming alliances with idolaters would pull God's people away from the truth. The Lord demanded uncompromised loyalty from His followers.

Pagan idolaters were not permitted to remain living within the land, because their presence would lead Israel into sin. Serving foreign gods would become a deadly trap for God's chosen people. To stay faithful to God, they needed to keep away from corrupting influences.
